Far side of the Moon — Wikipedia
Chang'e 4 lander · Yutu-2 rover (stationary since March 2024)

The first spacecraft to land on the Moon's far side — technically and operationally the hardest lunar landing ever attempted. Required a relay satellite (Queqiao) at L2 since the far side has no direct radio contact with Earth. Yutu-2 rover drove over 1.6 km before becoming stationary in March 2024; telemetry continued through at least September 2024. The far side had never been visited.
Demonstrated relay-satellite communications architecture for operations beyond direct line-of-sight — the exact pattern any Mars far-side or polar mission will need.

Chang'e 4 landed in Von Kármán Crater on January 3, 2019 — the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, where Earth is never visible. Communication was relayed via the Queqiao satellite parked at L2. Deployed Yutu-2 rover, which has driven 1.5+ km and is still operating in 2026, the longest-active lunar surface mission of all time. Found pristine mantle material in South Pole-Aitken basin.
First far-side lunar lander + L2 relay satellite (Queqiao)
Chang'e 4 lander + Yutu-2 rover during pre-launch integration in Beijing.
Queqiao L2 relay satellite — without it, Chang'e 4 would have no contact with Earth. China built lunar comms infrastructure before going far-side.
Von Kármán Crater, far side — landed January 3, 2019
Yutu-2 rover photographed by Chang'e 4 lander — first wheels on the far side of the Moon.
Yutu-2 inspects a glassy bead on the surface — likely an impact melt fragment from a distant cratering event.
Mantle material in South Pole-Aitken basin
VNIS spectra showed olivine + low-Ca pyroxene — minerals from the lunar mantle, exposed by the SPA basin impact ~4.2 billion years ago.

Illustrated block map of the Chang’e 4 landing site in Von Kármán crater: the Chang’e 4 lander stands in the east, the Yutu-2 position of May 2019 lies a short way west, and the rover’s route winds a long way west and north-west to its last position, marked by a small rover.
